newsitem.title: USA: Charges filed against six in Texas standoff.
newsitem.headline: Charges filed against six in Texas standoff.

text.p: Formal charges were filed on Monday against six members of an armed Texas separatist group amid signs that police were preparing to move in to put an end to a tense two-day standoff.

The threat of violence hung in the air as state, local and federal police officers poured into the remote west Texas region where the group, the Republic of Texas, holed up in a compound deep in the Davis Mountains. The group wants to make Texas an independent nation.

Texas Department of Public Safety spokeswoman Sherri Deatherage Green said the charges filed on Monday included engaging in an organised criminal activity and aggravated kidnapping with a deadly weapon.
Negotiators from the Texas Rangers were talking with the Republic members by phone trying to bring a peaceful end to the situation, she said.

But all signs pointed to anything but peace. Dozens of police cars rolled past reporters waiting at a DPS roadblock on the road to the Republic compound. Special weapons and tactics teams from the DPS and FBI were set up at staging grounds on nearby ranches for a possible showdown.

Deatherage Green said DPS officers had moved to within two miles (three kms) of the Republic compound. Two military vehicles were seen entering the area, but she said they were only bringing bedding for police.

The standoff began on Sunday when Republic security chief Robert Scheidt was arrested by the local sheriff for possession of illegal arms, including an AK-47 automatic weapon. In retaliation, the Republic took two neighbours hostage.
Police closed in and after 12 hours of negotiations, self- styled Republic leader Richard McLaren agreed to turn over the hostages in exchange for Scheidt's freedom.

Another DPS spokesman, Mike Cox, said negotiations had not progressed since the release. He said the Republic members were demanding the United Nations enter the fray to help Texas secede. News reports said a church pastor in nearly Alpine, Texas, was attempting to get former President Jimmy Carter to intercede.

Texas Attorney General Dan Morales expressed frustation with the Republic, which has stirred up trouble in the state for about two years. The Republic of Texas has a warrant out for the arrest of Morales, and for all the top government officials in the state.
"If they don't like it in Texas, they're free to leave ... no one is holding a gun to their head forcing them to stay," Morales told reporters.

Republic leaders say that Texas's 1845 annexation into the United States was unconstitutional and that it should declare its independence and put them in charge. Texas was an independent nation for nine years after it broke away from Mexico in 1836.

The Republic group set up its own court system and militia units, and has since filed thousands of liens against government agencies and private property owners. None of their activities have been recognised as legal by the state.

McLaren was charged with contempt last December for failing to appear in federal court in nearby Pecos, Texas, on charges related to the liens. Since then, he and several followers have holed up inside the compound, which is about 200 miles (321 km) southeast of El Paso, Texas, sending out their separatist message by fax and the Internet.
Police, mindful of the disastrous conclusion to similar standoffs at Ruby Ridge, Idaho, and the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, did not arrest McLaren to avoid sparking a violent clash.
But those fears may now be over. Cox told reporters that, despite McLaren's predictions, there were no signs that militia members from around the nation were coming to his aid.
Attorney Terence O'Rourke of Houston, who represents McLaren, told reporters the standoff had become dangerous. "It's obviously a situation that could turn violent at any time," he said.
